newsitem.title: FRANCE: Ship subsidy pact delayed again, U.S. blamed.
newsitem.headline: Ship subsidy pact delayed again, U.S. blamed.

text.p: A delayed international pact to scrap shipyard subsidies will remain on the shelf for at least five months because the United States has failed to ratify it, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development said on Friday.
Countries which signed the accord expressed concern in two days of talks at the refusal by Congress to ratify it, and urged each other not to get into a new subsidy war, the OECD said.

The pact between the United States, European Union, Japan, South Korea and Norway was meant to take effect in July and aims to stamp out most of the government subsidies and predatory pricing blamed for a lengthy shipbuilding slump.
Washington is the only capital which has not ratified the so-called Shipbuilding Trade Agreement Act as it stands.
The OECD, which brokered the accord, said signatories had agreed to meet again in March to receive a report by the United States on how the prospects for ratification were looking then.
The meeting would decide on "further action, if any, to be taken," an OECD statement said.
It warned that while the agreement was being held up, the shipbuilding industry was speeding towards even greater competition, with capacity growing faster than demand.
Delegates at the meeting had urged that "all signatories would refrain from actions aimed at creating unilateral advantages," the OECD said.

Washington has been roundly criticised for delaying the pact, which covers 80 percent of the world's shipyard capacity. The U.S. shipbuilding industry says it has not had time to adjust to the loss of military business after the Cold War.
The Clinton administration endorses the pact but approval was held up in June when the House of Representatives passed an amendment delaying U.S. implementation to January 1999.
A Senate initiative to exclude the amendment ran out of time before Congress adjourned.
Under the agreement the United States would phase out some of its $50 million a year in federally-backed loan guarantees to shipbuilders.
Virginia Republican Representative Herbert Bateman, author of the House amendment, said the delay was needed to match clauses that other countries had negotiated into the agreement.

The amendment also seeks to preserve the politically sensitive U.S. Jones Act, which prohibits cargo shipment between U.S. ports in foreign-built ships. The Clinton administration has said the Jones Act exemption was implicit in the agreement.

A spokesman for the EU's executive Commission said on Wednesday that U.S. ratification was being blocked "by strong vested interests which seek to benefit from large subsidies to re-enter the market for merchant vessels".
The EU in September extended its rules allowing shipbuilding aid until the end of 1997 if the OECD agreement stays dormant.
